explanation: The ejected organs can distract or entangle an attacker while the sea cucumber escapes. It then regrows the lost parts over the following weeks or months.

claims.text: Some sea cucumbers defend themselves by expelling some of their internal organs.
Sea urchins, starfish and hermit crabs do not defend themselves by ejecting their internal organs.
Expelled sea cucumber organs can distract or entangle a predator.
Sea cucumbers regrow expelled organs over a period of weeks or months.

evidence.restatement: Many sea cucumbers defend themselves by evisceration, expelling parts of the gut and other internal organs.
Sea urchins rely on spines, starfish can shed arms and hermit crabs retreat into shells; none of them ejects internal organs in defence.
The ejected organs, and in some species sticky Cuvierian tubules, distract or entangle a predator while the animal escapes.
Sea cucumbers regenerate the expelled organs, over several weeks to a few months depending on the species.
Some sea cucumbers push out part of their insides (gut, respiratory tree or sticky tubules) when attacked.
Sea urchins, starfish and hermit crabs do not defend themselves by ejecting internal organs (a starfish may drop an arm, which is a different thing).
Material expelled by a sea cucumber can entangle or distract a predator.
Eviscerated sea cucumbers regrow the lost organs within weeks to a few months.

stem: Which sea creature can defend itself by shooting out some of its own internal organs?
